record.paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
record.original_question: Do the similarities between manganites and other correlated materials such as organic superconductors and heavy-fermion compounds—especially phase competition, first-order transitions or coexistence, and a higher crossover scale T*—reflect a shared underlying phenomenology rather than accidental analogy?

evidence.quote: The similarities with results for manganites are strong: first-order transitions or phase coexistence, and the presence of a T*. It remains to be investigated whether the similarities are accidental or reveal the same phenomenology observed in competing phases of manganites.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider three families of strongly correlated electronic materials: (i) colossal-magnetoresistance manganites of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a rare earth and A a divalent alkaline earth), (ii) quasi–two-dimensional organic superconductors of the (BEDT-TTF) and (TMTSF) families, and (iii) heavy-fermion intermetallic compounds based on Ce, U or Yb. Across these families one observes the following common low-temperature phenomenology near a control parameter g (chemical doping, pressure, or magnetic field) that tunes between two competing electronic phases A and B (for example ferromagnetic-metallic versus charge/orbital-ordered insulating in manganites, antiferromagnetic-insulating versus superconducting in organics, antiferromagnetic versus heavy Fermi-liquid or superconducting in heavy fermions):

1. A first-order transition line, or an extended regime of mesoscopic phase coexistence between A and B, in the (g, T) phase diagram at low temperature.
2. A crossover temperature T*(g) substantially larger than the ordering temperatures of either pure phase, below which non-trivial short-range correlations, pseudogap features, or precursor inhomogeneities appear.
3. Strong sensitivity of bulk response functions (resistivity, susceptibility, specific heat) to quenched disorder near the boundary between A and B.

Question. Formulate and decide the following: does there exist a single universal effective theory — for instance a Ginzburg–Landau–Wilson functional with two competing order parameters φ_A, φ_B coupled to elastic strain and to quenched random-field disorder — whose phase diagram and finite-temperature crossovers simultaneously reproduce features (1)–(3) in all three families, with material-dependent parameters but family-independent universal exponents and scaling functions governing the coexistence region and the crossover scale T*? Equivalently, are the observed similarities (first-order transitions / phase coexistence and the higher crossover scale T*) manifestations of one shared underlying phenomenology of competing orders with disorder, or do they arise from microscopically distinct mechanisms that only superficially mimic each other?
artifact.status_search_result: The question of whether competing-phase phenomenology with first-order transitions, mesoscopic coexistence, and a higher crossover scale T* in manganites, organic superconductors, and heavy-fermion compounds reflects a single universal framework remains a topic of active debate. While substantial theoretical work (e.g., Dagotto and collaborators on competing-phase scenarios with quenched disorder, and the quantum-critical-point / competing-order paradigm for heavy fermions and organics) supports broad analogies, no rigorous universal effective theory has been established and accepted across all three families. The status is best described as open.

status_evidence.title: Phase separation and competing orders in manganites and related systems
status_evidence.snippet: It remains to be investigated whether the similarities are accidental or reveal the same phenomenology observed in competing phases of manganites.
status_evidence.claim: The unifying framework is posed as an open investigation.
